title: Hercules and the Waggoner
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Waggoner was driving his team along a muddy lane with a full load behind them, when the wheels of his waggon sank so deep in the mire that no efforts of his horses could move them. As he stood there, looking helplessly on, and calling loudly at intervals upon Hercules for assistance, the god himself appeared, and said to him, "Put your shoulder to the wheel, man, and goad on your horses, and then you may call on Hercules to assist you. If you won't lift a finger to help yourself, you can't expect Hercules or any one else to come to your aid."
Heaven helps those who help themselves.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Waggoner's wheels?
options: They break apart on a rocky path
They are stolen while he rests
They sink so deep in the mire that his horses cannot move them
They freeze solid in cold weather

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Waggoner do while standing looking on helplessly?
options: He calls loudly upon Hercules for assistance
He unloads the waggon by himself
He unhitches the horses and walks away
He asks a passing stranger for help

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who appears in answer to the Waggoner's calls?
options: A passing farmer
Another waggoner
A group of villagers
Hercules himself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Hercules tell the Waggoner to do first?
options: Wait patiently until the mud dries
Put his shoulder to the wheel and goad on his horses
Remove some of the load from the waggon
Pray again more sincerely for help

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Hercules say the Waggoner can do once he has tried himself?
options: Give up and leave the waggon behind
Ask a different god for help
Call on Hercules to assist him
Sell the horses and walk home

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Hercules say will happen if the Waggoner won't lift a finger to help himself?
options: He can't expect Hercules or anyone else to come to his aid
Hercules will still help him out of pity
The horses will eventually free the wheels alone
The gods will punish him for his laziness

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Hercules refuse to simply free the wheels himself?
options: He is unable to move the waggon himself
He is testing whether the Waggoner truly worships him
He believes the horses alone should solve the problem
He wants the Waggoner to make an effort before expecting outside help

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Waggoner's behavior before Hercules arrives suggest about his approach to the problem?
options: He has already tried everything possible before calling for help
He expects help to arrive without making any effort of his own
He believes Hercules will punish him for asking at all
He does not actually believe Hercules will respond

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "goad" mean in "goad on your horses"?
options: To feed or water
To untie or release
To urge or prompt into action
To praise or encourage gently

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Real help comes to those who first make an honest effort on their own behalf
Gods only assist those who never ask for their help
Waggoners should never travel on muddy roads
Calling loudly for help is the fastest way to solve a problem

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of load is the Waggoner carrying?
options: An empty waggon
A load of firewood only
A load too light to matter
A full load

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Waggoner get stuck?
options: On a steep hill
In a muddy lane
At a narrow bridge
In a rocky pass

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Hercules call the Waggoner while speaking to him?
options: "Friend"
"Fool"
"Man"
"Traveller"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might Hercules's response be seen as fair rather than harsh?
options: He is not refusing to help, only asking for effort before assistance is given
He never actually appears to speak to the Waggoner at all
He offers to do all the work if the Waggoner simply watches
He blames the Waggoner for choosing to travel that day

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what specific action does Hercules expect before he will help?
options: A formal prayer recited in the proper way
A sacrifice offered at a temple
A promise to travel only in dry weather from then on
Physical effort from the Waggoner himself, pushing and urging the horses on

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "mire" mean in "sank so deep in the mire"?
options: Loose gravel or stones
Deep mud or wet ground
Thick ice or frost
Dry sand or dust

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Hercules frees the Waggoner's wheels without saying a word
The Waggoner refuses to accept help even when it is offered
Hercules tells a Waggoner calling for help that he must first try to free the wheels himself
The horses free the wheels before Hercules arrives
